clinicalPearls: A severe presentation of Kawasaki disease in which children develop haemodynamic instability and hypotension requiring fluid resuscitation or inotropic support.

It should be considered in a child with features of Kawasaki disease (prolonged fever, mucocutaneous changes, conjunctival injection, extremity changes, rash, cervical lymphadenopathy) who also appears shocked.
Compared with classic Kawasaki disease, shock syndrome is more often associated with incomplete presentations, greater systemic inflammation, and a higher risk of coronary artery involvement.
Laboratory markers tend to show more intense inflammation, lower platelet counts, and evidence of consumptive or capillary-leak processes.
These children are more likely to be initially resistant to intravenous immunoglobulin and may need additional immunomodulatory therapy.
The overlap with toxic shock syndrome and septic shock frequently leads to diagnostic delay, so a high index of suspicion is essential.
Prompt echocardiography is important because of the elevated risk of coronary artery aneurysms and myocardial dysfunction.
Timely treatment of the underlying vasculitis, in addition to circulatory support, is key to reducing coronary complications.
reference.pathophysiology: Kawasaki disease is a self-limited medium-vessel vasculitis of childhood driven by intense systemic immune activation. In the shock variant, an exaggerated inflammatory response with high circulating cytokine levels produces vasodilation, myocardial dysfunction, and increased vascular permeability with capillary leak. The combination of impaired cardiac contractility and fluid shifts out of the intravascular space results in hypotension and organ hypoperfusion, superimposed on the vasculitic damage that threatens the coronary arteries.
additionalDifferentials: Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis with macrophage activation
Severe adenoviral or other viral infection
additionalInvestigations: Echocardiography to assess coronary arteries and ventricular function
Full blood count with attention to platelets and anaemia
Serum albumin, sodium, and liver function tests
Blood cultures and infection screen to exclude sepsis and toxic shock
redFlags: Hypotension or shock requiring fluids or inotropes (EMERGENCY)
Signs of myocardial dysfunction or heart failure
Evidence of coronary artery aneurysm on echocardiography
Rapidly rising inflammatory markers with falling platelets
Multi-organ hypoperfusion or deteriorating conscious level
reference.prognosis: With early recognition and treatment most children recover, but the shock variant carries a higher rate of coronary artery abnormalities, myocardial dysfunction, and immunoglobulin resistance than classic disease, so outcomes depend on prompt immunomodulation and cardiac follow-up.
pitfalls: Mislabelling the presentation as septic or toxic shock and delaying Kawasaki-directed treatment
Missing incomplete or atypical Kawasaki features in a shocked child
Aggressive fluid loading without recognising myocardial dysfunction
Assuming a single dose of immunoglobulin has controlled the disease without monitoring for resistance
Neglecting early and repeat echocardiography for coronary surveillance
management: Prompt intravenous immunoglobulin as the mainstay immunomodulatory therapy to quell inflammation and protect the coronary arteries
Adjunctive corticosteroids given the high rate of immunoglobulin resistance in the shock variant, escalating to infliximab, ciclosporin or anakinra for refractory inflammation
Anti-inflammatory aspirin during the acute febrile phase transitioning to antiplatelet aspirin once fever settles
Fluid resuscitation with vasoactive and inotropic support and intensive care admission for the haemodynamic instability and capillary leak
Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics until septic shock and toxic shock syndrome are excluded, given the diagnostic overlap
Serial echocardiography to detect and monitor coronary artery aneurysms and myocardial dysfunction
Thromboprophylaxis with antiplatelet therapy and anticoagulation if giant coronary aneurysms develop
Paediatric cardiology and intensive care multidisciplinary follow-up with long-term coronary surveillance
